promptText: What is the key difference between fine-tuning and prompt engineering?
options: Fine-tuning permanently updates the model's weights using a task-specific dataset, so behavior persists across all future calls without repeating instructions; prompt engineering only shapes behavior for requests that include the crafted prompt, changing nothing in the model
Fine-tuning and prompt engineering both modify the model's weights, differing only in how many examples are used
Prompt engineering requires GPU training infrastructure, while fine-tuning can be done by editing a text string
Fine-tuning only works on closed-source hosted models, while prompt engineering only works on open-weight models
explanation: Fine-tuning converts a recurring, per-request instruction cost into a one-time, offline training cost by moving knowledge and behavior out of the prompt and into the weights.

promptText: Why can fine-tuning datasets be dramatically smaller than pretraining datasets (hundreds of examples vs. trillions of tokens)?
options: The base model already learned general language competence and broad world knowledge during pretraining; fine-tuning only needs to nudge that already-capable model toward a narrower behavior, not build capability from scratch
Fine-tuning datasets are compressed using a special tokenizer that represents each example as thousands of equivalent tokens
Small datasets are purely a limitation of current fine-tuning APIs, and larger datasets always produce strictly better results with no tradeoff
Fine-tuning does not use gradient descent, so dataset size does not affect how well the model learns
explanation: This is the transfer-learning premise: you are not training a language model from scratch, you are nudging an already-capable one toward a narrower shift in style, format, or domain behavior.

promptText: A team wants to fine-tune a model to reliably cite the company's current product prices. Why is this generally a poor use of fine-tuning?
options: Prices change frequently, and fine-tuning bakes information into weights at a fixed point in time -- every price change would require a full retraining cycle, whereas RAG can inject current facts at request time from an easily updated store
Fine-tuning cannot represent numeric values in its output at all, regardless of the domain
Fine-tuning is only capable of changing tone and voice, never any content related to numbers
This is actually the ideal use case for fine-tuning, since prices are simple facts that are trivial to memorize permanently
explanation: Fine-tuning to teach facts instead of behavior is the single most common and most expensive mistake in this space -- frequently changing facts belong in retrieval, not baked into weights.

promptText: What is 'catastrophic forgetting' in the context of fine-tuning?
options: Training a model on a new, narrow task causes it to lose or degrade abilities it previously had, because the same weights that encoded those old abilities got overwritten while learning the new task
The permanent deletion of a fine-tuning dataset after training completes, making the fine-tune impossible to reproduce
A model's tendency to forget the current conversation's history after each individual turn
The process by which a provider retires an old base model version, forcing customers to re-fine-tune
explanation: A model fine-tuned heavily on one narrow behavior might become noticeably worse at general reasoning or coding tasks it used to handle fine, even though the fine-tuning task never explicitly touched those skills.

promptText: What distinguishes a 'base model' from an 'instruct' or 'chat' model?
options: A base model is the raw output of pretraining with no particular tendency to follow instructions; an instruct/chat model is that same model after additional fine-tuning stages (instruction tuning, usually RLHF or DPO) aimed at making it follow directions and converse helpfully
A base model only supports single-word outputs, while a chat model supports full sentences
A base model is always smaller in parameter count than the corresponding chat model
There is no meaningful difference; the terms are interchangeable marketing labels for the same artifact
explanation: A raw base model may continue a question with more questions, since that pattern is common in raw text; instruction tuning specifically teaches the behavior of interpreting text as a request and responding helpfully.

promptText: What does PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) refer to as an umbrella term?
options: A family of techniques, including LoRA, adapters, and prompt/prefix tuning, that update only a small subset of a model's parameters (or add a small number of new ones) instead of updating every weight
A technique that fine-tunes a model using exclusively synthetic, LLM-generated training data
A method for compressing a fine-tuned model's file size after full fine-tuning has already completed
A regulatory framework governing which categories of data may be used in a fine-tuning dataset
explanation: The shared goal across all PEFT techniques is getting most of the behavioral benefit of full fine-tuning at a small fraction of the memory, compute, and storage cost.

promptText: How does LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) modify a model during fine-tuning?
options: It freezes the entire pretrained weight matrix W and injects small trainable low-rank matrices A and B alongside it, so the effective weight becomes W + B*A, with only A and B receiving gradient updates
It removes a fixed percentage of the model's parameters entirely before training begins, then retrains only the remaining ones
It duplicates every weight matrix in the model and averages the two copies after each training step
It converts all of the model's weights to a lower numerical precision as its sole mechanism for reducing training cost
explanation: LoRA constrains the update to a low-rank correction on top of the original weight, betting that the behavioral shift needed for most fine-tuning tasks lives in a much lower-dimensional space than the full weight matrix.

promptText: Why does a LoRA adapter typically carry a lower risk of catastrophic forgetting than full fine-tuning?
options: The original pretrained weights are frozen and never updated, so the base knowledge stays intact; only the small added adapter matrices change, limiting how much the model's prior behavior can be disturbed
LoRA adapters are incapable of learning anything beyond formatting rules, so they cannot possibly affect any other capability
LoRA runs for more training epochs than full fine-tuning, which mathematically guarantees better generalization
Catastrophic forgetting is a myth that only appears in full fine-tuning marketing materials, not a real measurable phenomenon
explanation: Full fine-tuning moves every weight and can erode general capability through broad weight movement, while LoRA's frozen base weights mean base knowledge stays intact even as the adapter learns the new behavior.

promptText: What is DPO (Direct Preference Optimization), and why do many teams prefer it over full RLHF?
options: DPO reformulates preference learning as a direct, supervised-style loss computed straight from (chosen, rejected) response pairs, avoiding the need for a separate reward model and an unstable reinforcement-learning loop that RLHF requires
DPO trains exclusively on single correct-answer labels and has no concept of comparing two responses at all
DPO is identical to instruction tuning and was simply renamed for marketing purposes
DPO requires more GPU memory than RLHF because it must store two full copies of the reward model simultaneously
explanation: DPO achieves the same preference-alignment goal as RLHF with meaningfully less infrastructure and tuning effort, which is why it has become the more common default outside frontier-lab-scale efforts.

promptText: Why does a multi-tenant fine-tuning platform typically default to LoRA-style adapters rather than full fine-tuning per customer?
options: Hosting N full fine-tuned models scales memory and GPU cost linearly with N and becomes economically unworkable past a small number of tenants, while one shared base model plus N small hot-swappable adapters scales far more gracefully
Full fine-tuning is technically incapable of being deployed behind an API endpoint, unlike LoRA adapters
LoRA adapters always produce strictly higher task accuracy than full fine-tuning regardless of dataset size
Regulatory requirements legally prohibit full fine-tuning in any multi-tenant SaaS product
explanation: Memory footprint at serving time is frequently the deciding factor between full fine-tuning and PEFT in a real platform architecture decision, independent of training cost.

promptText: What is 'reward hacking' in the RLHF context, and how would you detect it?
options: The model learns to score highly against the reward model's proxy signal (e.g., by being longer or more agreeable) without genuinely improving in the way the reward model was meant to measure -- detected by comparing reward-model score trends against a separate human-graded quality check on a held-out sample
A security vulnerability where an attacker directly edits a model's reward function file to grant themselves elevated API access
The practice of intentionally lowering a model's reward score to make it appear more cautious in benchmarks
A hardware fault that occurs when GPUs used for RLHF training overheat during long training runs
explanation: If the reward score keeps climbing while genuine human-judged quality plateaus or declines, that gap is the signature of reward hacking, usually calling for retraining or diversifying the reward model.

promptText: A fine-tune performs suspiciously well on inputs resembling its training examples but fails on slightly different phrasing. What is the most likely cause, and what is the correct fix?
options: Overfitting from insufficient training-data diversity -- the model memorized surface phrasing rather than the underlying task logic; the fix is expanding the dataset with varied phrasings and edge cases, not training longer on the same data
The base model itself lacks the capability to ever generalize, so no amount of additional data would help; the only fix is switching to a fundamentally different model architecture
The evaluation set was too large, and the fix is to shrink it down to only the examples the model already handles correctly
This is expected, optimal behavior for any fine-tuned model and requires no further action
explanation: This is the classic overfitting signature; more training on the same narrow data typically makes it worse, while deliberately varied phrasings and structures teach the underlying pattern instead of surface memorization.

promptText: Applying the 'brilliant new hire' heuristic from this chapter, how do you decide whether a persistent quality problem is a prompting/RAG issue versus a genuine fine-tuning problem?
options: If a competent new hire given the current instructions and a few examples would get the task right immediately, it's a prompting or retrieval problem; if they would need extensive repeated practice to internalize the behavior despite clear instructions and correct information being present, that signals the model's default behavioral tendencies need to shift -- a genuine fine-tuning problem
Any problem that persists after one round of prompt editing should automatically be escalated to fine-tuning, since prompting is assumed to be exhausted after a single attempt
The heuristic states that fine-tuning is always the correct first step, and prompting should only be tried if fine-tuning fails
The heuristic applies only to classification tasks and provides no guidance for open-ended generation tasks
explanation: This heuristic signals mature judgment about when NOT to fine-tune -- it distinguishes a problem solvable by better instructions from one that requires genuinely shifting the model's behavioral tendencies through weight updates.

promptText: A platform serves fine-tuned behavior for many enterprise customers and must choose between full fine-tuning and LoRA adapters. Beyond raw training cost, what is the deciding architectural factor at scale, and why?
options: Serving-time memory footprint: hosting N full model copies scales memory linearly with N and becomes economically unworkable past a small number of tenants, while one shared base model plus N small hot-swappable adapters scales far more gracefully -- this, not training-time cost, is usually what makes or breaks the platform's economics
The deciding factor is always the size of the training dataset per customer, since larger customer datasets mechanically require full fine-tuning regardless of serving architecture
Full fine-tuning and LoRA have identical serving-time memory profiles, so the choice is purely a matter of training speed
LoRA adapters cannot be versioned or rolled back independently, so full fine-tuning is required for any platform needing per-tenant rollback
explanation: A multi-tenant platform should default to parameter-efficient methods specifically because serving-time economics, not training-time economics, are what make or break the business model at scale.

promptText: LoRA's empirical bet is that a low-rank correction (rank 8-64) is often enough to meaningfully shift a large model's behavior. What does this imply about the relationship between rank, catastrophic forgetting risk, and the scope of achievable behavioral change?
options: Because the update is constrained to a low-dimensional correction added on top of frozen original weights, the base model's broad knowledge stays largely undisturbed (lower forgetting risk), but this same constraint means LoRA is best suited to behavioral shifts that genuinely live in a low-dimensional space (style, format, narrow skills) rather than pervasive, large-scale capability changes
Rank has no relationship to forgetting risk at all; LoRA and full fine-tuning carry identical forgetting risk regardless of the update's dimensionality
A higher rank always eliminates catastrophic forgetting entirely, so production teams should always maximize rank regardless of task
Low-rank updates can only be applied to the model's embedding layer and have no effect on attention projection matrices
explanation: The same property that makes LoRA safer (frozen base weights, low-dimensional correction) also bounds what kind of behavioral change it can efficiently express -- large, pervasive shifts spread throughout the network are a better fit for full fine-tuning.
